findings.body: `first_sentence` uses `.find(". ")` to locate sentence boundaries, but a sentence may end with a period without a following space (e.g., at the end of the input or before a closing quote). That case falls through to returning the whole string, which is fine, but the function is also blind to periods adjacent to non-space characters like newlines, carriage returns, or punctuation. This means model-authored text with lines separated by `\n` or ending mid-sentence will not be truncated correctly. Also, a period immediately before a quote character (e.g., `".") would also be missed. Consider using a regex or a more robust boundary detection that accounts for common sentence-ending punctuation and whitespace.
findings.title: Handle period followed by non-space or end-of-string

findings.body: When `shorten` truncates on a word boundary, it produces a string of length `space + 1` (because `…` is one character) while the caller expects at most `limit` characters. The `limit` parameter is used as the character count before the ellipsis, so the result can be `limit + 1` characters (when no space is found, `space` is `limit`). The tests only check `<= 21` for `limit=20`, which accepts outputs of 21. If the caller (e.g., GitHub's check-run title) enforces a strict maximum, this could cause truncation. Replace the ellipsis with a '…' only when it fits, or trim further when adding the ellipsis would exceed the limit.
findings.title: Ellipsis may push output over limit

findings.body: The `shorten` function uses `rfind(' ')` to find the last word boundary before the limit. In many scripts (Japanese, Chinese, Thai) words are not separated by spaces, so `rfind(' ')` returns `None` and the function appends an ellipsis mid-word. This is already tested with `日本語のタイトルはとても長いのです`, which is 15 characters and fits within the 20 limit, so the test does not exercise the issue. For a future iteration, consider using Unicode line-breaking rules (via `unicode-linebreak` crate) or at least document this limitation.
findings.title: Consider non-space word boundaries

findings.body: The docker-compose file sets `TINYSWEEPER_APP_PRIVATE_KEY`, but the repository's server code reads `TINYSWEEPER_GITHUB_PRIVATE_KEY` (this is apparent from the diff's comment noting the old spelling was never read). The change fixes the spelling, but now the variable name is `TINYSWEEPER_APP_PRIVATE_KEY` while other GitHub-related variables in the compose file use `TINYSWEEPER_APP_ID`. The codebase convention (from `server::auth::AppAuth::from_env`) is `TINYSWEEPER_APP_ID` and `TINYSWEEPER_APP_PRIVATE_KEY`. This is a correct fix, but the body of the finding is that the same convention must be reflected in the code that reads them – this is already done in the diff, so this is a non-issue. Rethinking: The actual issue is that the diff removes `TINYSWEEPER_GITHUB_APP_ID` and `TINYSWEEPER_GITHUB_PRIVATE_KEY` and adds `TINYSWEEPER_APP_ID` and `TINYSWEEPER_APP_PRIVATE_KEY`. If the server code expects `TINYSWEEPER_APP_ID` and `TINYSWEEPER_APP_PRIVATE_KEY`, that is fine. However, the repository's own instructions say: "Secrets found are reported by type and location only; value never reaches comments, summaries, or logs." This is not about secrets, so ignore. I'll keep this as a low-severity finding for potential mismatch if the codebase hasn't been fully updated, but the diff does that update. Actually, the diff changes the compose file and the server code (not visible in this diff). I'll assume the server code is correctly reading the new names. The finding is about an environment variable name that may have been missed elsewhere. But that is speculative. Better to remove this finding. I'll replace it with nothing and keep findings only from the summarise module.
findings.existing_code: TINYSWEEPER_APP_PRIVATE_KEY: ${TINYSWEEPER_APP_PRIVATE_KEY:?set the GitHub App private key}
findings.title: Rename environment variable to match codebase convention

value.summary: This pull request adds infrastructure for local development and a text-shortening helper. It is experimental, not for merging as stated, and the findings are about correctness and consistency in `first_sentence` and an environment variable spelling.
